findings.title: Run deletion stayed fully serial while listing and upload were parallelized for the identical scale problem
findings.suggested_fix: _walk_keys (line 543) enumerates keys with a plain recursive generator and _delete_prefix's delete_objects loop (lines 530-540) issues its 1000-key batches one at a time in a for loop -- both purely sequential. removeModelRun (controllers.py:271) calls run_store.delete() synchronously inside the HTTP request/response cycle, and the portal serves on one uvicorn worker by default, so for the stated 8,105-catchment/36,000-file run this is roughly 36 sequential LIST pages plus 36 sequential delete_objects calls (~70+ network round trips) blocking every other user of the portal for the whole deletion. The commit already has the pattern to fix this: parallelize the delete_objects chunk submissions with the same ThreadPoolExecutor/UPLOAD-style bounded pool used in _cached_listing and _upload_directory (chunks are independent, so this is safe), and/or run large deletions off the request thread (background job with a polled status, mirroring ingest's job pattern) rather than inline in removeModelRun. Enumeration can also be pipelined against deletion instead of materializing the full key list first, though that is a smaller win than parallelizing the batches.

findings.title: Listing concurrency (16) and upload concurrency (16, doubled by MAX_CONCURRENT_INGESTS=2) exceed botocore's default connection pool of 10
findings.suggested_fix: LISTING_CONCURRENCY defaults to 16 (run_store.py:62) and UPLOAD_CONCURRENCY defaults to 16 (ingest.py:50, used at ingest.py:302); with MAX_CONCURRENT_INGESTS=2 (controllers.py) two ingests can run 32 upload threads against one process's boto3 client. No STORAGES/Config entry in this repo sets max_pool_connections, so unless the deployment's ngiab_runs/default storage OPTIONS raise it, botocore's urllib3 pool defaults to 10 connections. Concurrency beyond that doesn't error, but urllib3 discards and re-opens connections past the pool size (logging 'Connection pool is full, discarding connection'), adding a fresh TCP+TLS handshake per excess request and eroding much of the concurrency benefit this commit is trying to buy. Either lower the two *_CONCURRENCY defaults to <=10, or explicitly configure a larger botocore Config(max_pool_connections=...) on the S3 storage backend(s) so the pool actually matches the thread count.

residual_risks: ThreadPoolExecutor is re-created on every _cached_listing cache miss (each 10s TTL rollover). Construction itself is cheap and OS thread spawn for up to 16 threads is low-single-digit milliseconds -- not material at any run count observed in this codebase (2 to a few hundred runs); not flagged as a finding.

boto3 clients (and the django-storages backends built on them) are documented thread-safe for concurrent calls from one shared client instance, which is how both _cached_listing and _upload_directory use them (one `storage()`/backend object, many threads calling save()/open()). This is the load-bearing assumption for both new pools and it holds.

The per-call closure and try/except added by _with_fresh_credentials (duckdb_conn.py query/fetchone) is noise: closure allocation and an unhit except are on the order of tens of nanoseconds against a ~9ms parquet read measured elsewhere in this file's own docstring -- not measurable in practice.

manifest.json being uploaded alone after the concurrent pool drains (ingest.py _upload_directory) adds exactly one extra synchronous PUT after however many parallel PUTs preceded it; trivial next to the total upload time for a multi-GB run.

_describe parsing JSON inside listing's worker threads is CPU work under the GIL, but manifest.json is small (kilobytes) and dominated by the network read that precedes it; the GIL does not meaningfully limit the observed I/O-bound speedup.

_walk_keys materializing every key before deleting costs roughly tens of bytes per key -- for 36,000 files, low single-digit megabytes. Not a memory concern; the cost that matters is the round trips (see the P1 finding above), not the memory.
testing_gaps: No test exercises _delete_prefix's boto3 batching at all: nothing asserts delete_objects is called in chunks of <=1000, that keys are correctly prefixed by backend.location, that Quiet=True is honored, or that the per-key fallback (no client / no bucket_name) still fires when a boto3 client isn't available. The entire object-storage delete path added in this commit has zero coverage (test_run_removal.py only exercises the local filesystem path via populated_root).

test_a_listing_spanning_several_pages_returns_every_entry (test_run_store.py) drives 1500 runs through the new ThreadPoolExecutor path incidentally, but nothing asserts LISTING_CONCURRENCY is actually respected (e.g. via a max-workers spy) or verifies behavior when one of many concurrent _describe calls raises StorageUnreachable partway through the pool.map.

_upload_directory's 'await every future before re-raising the first failure' fix (the specific race the docstring calls out -- a sibling upload writing after cleanup has already swept the prefix) is only tested with a 2-file fixture (test_publish_atomicity.py::test_a_failed_upload_removes_what_it_wrote) against a synchronous _Recorder fake, which never actually contends 16 real threads. No test drives more items than UPLOAD_CONCURRENCY with a slow/failing item to prove the race is closed under real thread scheduling.

No test covers the interaction between MAX_CONCURRENT_INGESTS and UPLOAD_CONCURRENCY (i.e. that two simultaneous ingests each running 16 upload threads is an accepted/expected load), which is the scenario behind the connection-pool finding above.
